Amara Knox

life-060 · holdout · fictional age 16

Written life first, then interpreted by a separate response author without the engine or results. These are synthetic checks. There is no correct career answer key.

Life from age 4 to 16

I like asking the questions more than being the interview subject. I want people to remember access before I arrive, so I can spend more time thinking about the same interesting things everyone else came for.

  • family: Lives with parents and a younger sister; everyone has household tasks and negotiates who needs assistance with what.
  • finances: Middle income from legal support and equipment sales; accessibility costs influence housing and travel decisions.
  • geography: Georgetown, Texas, in an accessible single-story house.
  • cultureLanguages: Black American family with English at home and close relationships across several Texas cities.
  • school: Public high school; fictional cerebral palsy affects lower-body mobility, and she uses a wheelchair with an accessibility and transport plan.
  • accessOpportunities: Accessible school media spaces and family advocacy offer opportunities; some off-campus venues still require advance checking.
  • Age 4–5

    Amara loved sorting costume jewelry and announcing pretend auctions with extravagant descriptions. Her wheelchair was part of daily movement, while her family’s clearest memory from that period was how seriously she took imaginary bidding rules.

  • Age 6–7

    At school she enjoyed reading aloud and making classmates laugh with dramatic character voices. A playground redesign let her join more games, and she insisted on helping choose rules instead of only being assigned a spectator role.

  • Age 8–9

    She started photographing neighborhood details from angles adults overlooked. A relative gave her a small camera, and she discovered that an ordinary curb or window could look different when she waited for the right light.

  • Age 10–11

    During remote learning she made a family photo archive and interviewed relatives by phone. She liked their stories but learned to ask permission before sharing photographs, especially when someone’s favorite memory involved another person’s embarrassment.

  • Age 12–13

    Joining the school news team introduced caption editing and careful fact checking. She enjoyed preparing an interview more than being on camera, though classmates sometimes pushed her toward public inspiration stories she had never volunteered to tell.

  • Age 14–15

    Amara helped evaluate access for a school trip while another student handled the main itinerary. The trip went well, but she resented the extra planning labor and asked adults to make access checks a standard responsibility next time.

  • Age 16

    She edits school news, takes photographs, and attends occasional accessible recreation sessions. She is investigating Texas study options through actual routes and housing details, while keeping questions about courses and friendships equally central to her decisions.

Life now

  • enjoys: Photographic light · Interview preparation · Character voices
  • avoids: Unrequested inspiration stories · Always owning access logistics
  • activities: School news · Photography · Accessible recreation
  • demonstratedSkills: Checks factual details · Organizes archives · Conducts respectful interviews
  • unfamiliarActivities: Ceramics · Advanced coding · Overnight independent travel
  • motivations: Accurate representation · Ordinary freedom to participate
  • ambitions: Wants further education and independent housing · Imagines a connected neighborhood where getting out to meet friends takes little negotiation.
  • struggles: Extra planning work · Others underestimating her range
  • supports: Family · Media adviser · Access coordinator · Friends
  • practicalConstraints: Accessible transportation and housing · Venue checks · Physical fatigue on long days

Still uncertain: Would she enjoy reporting unfamiliar or contentious subjects? · Which environments distribute access work reliably?
